summary: The per-reading invariants hold: both validators refuse NO_AT_CUTOFF while now < cutoff (resolution.py:125, :245) and both fired in the live corpus (group_coordination c258, holiday_deposit c575); the verifier is built from its own prompt on a stateless caller and carries no verdict, citation or explanation of the first reading (verified against all 14 verifier prompts in final_v6); disagreement never resolves into an answer (3 recorded, none claimed); every cited id in all 8 YES runs is a committed journal event of that trajectory, before the cutoff; and no terminal role can schedule or advance anything. The structural claim does not hold. All three scheduling sites refuse any instant past the cutoff (trajectory.py:215, :384; adapter.py:98-108), so the queue can never hold an item beyond it, so `ev.t > cutoff` (trajectory.py:841) and `reached_horizon` (:871) are dead and NO_AT_CUTOFF is reachable only when the last thing scheduled lands EXACTLY on the cutoff instant -- I reproduced this: the same world with wakes every 1/2/7 days or 6h answers NO, and every 3/4/5 days or 36h answers `incomplete_empty_queue`. In the corpus: 548 scheduled events, none past a cutoff; 0 horizon records; 0 of 209 judge calls final. Asked whether the three `incomplete_empty_queue` runs are honest: no -- the rule has overcorrected. They lived 92.3%, 98.8% and 99.2% of their windows, ended with an empty queue after every actor was asked and declined, and in two of them the actors' stated next moves lay past the deadline and were silently deleted by trajectory.py:215 -- which is the very state the code says licenses a NO. Deleting `empty queue => NO` was right; replacing it with `did the clock land on the cutoff instant` is not, because the scenarios whose true answer is NO are exactly the ones that empty the queue. Separately, an incomplete run CAN still answer NO (probe: max_steps=14 gives status=incomplete_step_limit, answer=NO_AT_CUTOFF), so the invariant I was asked to confirm is false in general.

findings.title: The horizon that licenses a NO is unreachable except by arithmetic coincidence, so 0 NO_AT_CUTOFF measures divisibility rather than the world
findings.evidence: sworldmodel/semantic_runtime/trajectory.py:215 (`if due > cutoff ... return False`), :384 (`if due <= cutoff:` else dropped), adapter.py:98-108 (`elif when <= cutoff`) are the only three scheduling sites, so no queue item can ever have t > cutoff; therefore trajectory.py:841 `ev.t > cutoff` never fires and :871 `reached_horizon["yes"] = ev is not None` is always False, making :785-793 (advance to cutoff + OP_HORIZON) and the NO branch at :1018-1030 reachable only when the clock already sits exactly on the cutoff. Corpus: 548 `event.scheduled` records across artifacts/final_v6, 0 beyond a cutoff; 0 `semantic.horizon_reached` records; 0 of 209 `semantic.terminal_check` records with final=True. Probe (scratchpad/th_probe_no.py, scripted transport, no provider, the 14-day scene from tests/test_semantic_runtime.py): wake every 1 day / 2 days / 7 days / 6 hours -> status=cutoff, answer=NO_AT_CUTOFF; wake every 3 days / 4 days / 5 days / 36 hours -> status=incomplete_empty_queue, answer=UNRESOLVED, identical world behaviour.
findings.why_it_matters: The headline `0 NO_AT_CUTOFF` is presented as a property of the corpus and the report frames the gap as one the runtime `cannot presently` close. It is structural: whether a run can answer NO is decided by whether its last scheduled instant happens to divide the window, not by what happened, and no number of new scenarios or better model outputs will change that. The comment at trajectory.py:1021-1025 (`A run whose next scheduled thing falls beyond the cutoff is the other case and keeps its NO`) describes a state the same file makes impossible, and tests/test_runtime_completion.py:85-107, the only test asserting the honest NO still works, passes solely because its window (14 days) is an exact multiple of its wake interval (2 days) -- change that interval to 3 days and it becomes an incomplete. The prior report named the missing mechanism (a wake because a deadline is coming); this branch deleted that provenance name (`known_deadline`, removed from WAKE_PROVENANCE at trajectory.py:154-155) as dead code without wiring anything in its place.
findings.suggested_fix: Define the horizon by the state rather than the instant -- nothing scheduled lands before the cutoff AND every actor was asked at the current instant and intends nothing before it -- or let the deadline itself schedule one item at exactly the cutoff, so `finish("")` is reached on purpose instead of by divisibility.

findings.title: The three incomplete runs are refused NOs, not unfinished trajectories: the rule has overcorrected
findings.evidence: holiday_deposit: lived 74.77h of a 75.33h window (99.2%), stopped 33m59s short; £400 reached Marian (e519), Nina's £200 went to Ruth and was transferred back (e1290), Marian saw the £600 had not arrived (e1321) and crossed the week out of her diary (e1383, 22:26Z); at 21:40Z marian_prowse's next_wake `2 hours` (due 23:40Z, cutoff 22:59:59Z) was dropped by trajectory.py:215. cold_email: lived 332.01h of 336h (98.8%), stopped 3h59m short; the email was delivered (e20) and never observed across 54 world adjudications; the last actor turns are `Nothing has changed; I already consider this a dead end` and `It's been two weeks... I don't intend to follow up`, both with next_wake None. evidence_avoiding: lived 96h of 104h (92.3%), stopped 8h short; at the final forced sweep 2026-09-11T08:00Z dana_whitfield's accepted reply carried next_wake `3 days` and marcus_bell's `3 days` -- both past the 16:00Z cutoff, both silently dropped. All three report reason `nothing further was scheduled ... and the cutoff ... was never reached`.
findings.why_it_matters: The runtime already accepts `nothing lands before the cutoff` as sufficient for a NO -- that is exactly what the reached_horizon branch is for. An empty queue after a completed forced sweep is the same epistemic state and arguably a stronger one, since the beyond-cutoff wake case at least means somebody intended something. The only difference is whether an actor happened to name an instant on the far side of the deadline, and code deletes precisely that datum before anything can see it (see the MEDIUM below). So the distinction the rule draws is an artifact, not an epistemic one -- and because the questions whose true answer is NO are exactly the ones in which nobody schedules anything (a man with his phone off, a cold email nobody opens, a deposit that does not arrive), the class of scenarios the runtime refuses to answer is the class it most needs to answer. For contrast, on merged main the same rule change would also have refused `delayed_response`, which reached its NO having lived 95.4% of its window, while correctly refusing `cold_email`, which had lived 21.4%: the discriminating quantity is how much of the window was lived and whether anyone still intended anything, and the new rule discards it.
findings.suggested_fix: Report the horizon as reached -- and permit NO -- when the queue is empty, every actor has been asked at the current instant, and no actor or world process intends anything before the cutoff; keep `incomplete_empty_queue` for the case the rule was written for, where the queue empties with the window substantially unlived.

findings.title: An incomplete run can still answer NO_AT_CUTOFF, and the reason string asserts a time relation it never checks
findings.evidence: trajectory.py:764-783 documents `it may never return NO, because that would turn a budget artifact into an answer`, but :794 passes `final=not truncated` only, and the sole guard is the clock test at resolution.py:125 / :245, which is false the moment now == cutoff. Probe (scratchpad/th_probe_trunc.py, scripted transport, no provider, wakes every 1 day so step 14 lands the clock on the cutoff): max_steps=14 returns status=`incomplete_step_limit`, answer=`NO_AT_CUTOFF`, reason=`step ceiling 14 reached at 2026-08-10T14:00:00+00:00, before the cutoff` -- the printed instant IS the cutoff (trajectory.py:1011-1012 and :1015-1016 hardcode `before the cutoff`). tests/test_semantic_runtime.py:1165-1187 cannot catch it (the judge is scripted `[UNRESOLVED] * 60`, so the assertion `traj.answer["status"] == "UNRESOLVED"  # never NO_AT_CUTOFF` is guaranteed by the script) and tests/test_runtime_completion.py:77-82 only tries steps 1, 2 and 3 against a silent world.
findings.why_it_matters: This is PR #5's defect in its original form -- a run that stopped because it ran out of budget reporting a deadline that passed -- surviving in the branch written to eliminate it, gated only by whether the truncation happens to land on the cutoff instant. The same arithmetic that makes an honest NO nearly unreachable makes this dishonest NO reachable. No run in final_v6 hit it, so the corpus is clean, but the invariant the branch is built on does not hold and the two tests named after it do not test it.
findings.suggested_fix: Pass `truncated` into make_validator/make_verifier_validator and reject NO_AT_CUTOFF whenever the run is incomplete, independently of the clock; and derive the `before the cutoff` wording from an actual comparison.

findings.title: A candidate YES is re-proposed until the two readings coincide, and only agreement stops the run
findings.evidence: trajectory.py:1002-1008 re-judges after any new committed event; :723-738 returns immediately on agreement but merely continues on disagreement. feedback_deadline: judge YES at 2026-07-28T13:34 rejected by verifier c133 (`she only composed and sent the email at the current time`); re-proposed at 13:36 and accepted (c143) with exactly one new committed event in between, e333 `Aline continues reading the thesis chapter and typing comments for about 30 minutes, reaching near the end of the document` -- which does not answer the objection and sits oddly with the claim she had already finished and sent at 13:34. group_coordination: judge YES at 2026-10-09T10:01 rejected by verifier c259 on the ground that `Tomas's final confirmation has not been observed by all`; re-proposed at 13:00 and accepted (c284) while the cited e532 is still observed_by=[ines, tomas] only, the new event e585 being Ines -- who had already agreed -- checking her phone. Bea never observed e510 (Kwame's acceptance) or e532 in the whole run.
findings.why_it_matters: `A terminal is accepted only when both agree` is true per attempt but weaker than it reads: with N committed events after a candidate, the pair gets up to N independent chances at temperature 0.7, the verifier has no memory of its own prior objection, and only YES ends the run -- so the stopping rule is a one-sided race to the first agreement, which is the same shape as the defect that sank PR #5 (ask again until an answer you can act on appears). Two of the eight shipped YES verdicts were produced this way, and group_coordination's is the one YES in the corpus whose status I would contest on its own record: `the four housemates settle on who hosts` is not established for Bea.
findings.suggested_fix: Hold a rejected candidate until the record changes in the respect the verifier objected to -- e.g. carry the objection forward and require the next reading to answer it -- instead of re-opening the pair on any new event.

findings.title: A stated 'later' that falls past the deadline is deleted with no record, and the run then reports that nothing was scheduled
findings.evidence: trajectory.py:215 `if due > cutoff or due <= world.clock.now: return False` emits no trace note, and both callers ignore the result (:404-406 for world processes, :501-508 for an actor's own plan); trace.py:98-99 writes only `wake_scheduled`, so grounded_wakes.jsonl records successes only, and the world's dropped events are noted (`event_beyond_cutoff`, trajectory.py:398) but written to no jsonl artifact -- only rendered into trajectory.md prose (trace.py:198-200). Dropped in final_v6: evidence_avoiding 2026-09-11T08:00Z dana_whitfield `3 days` and `1 day`, marcus_bell `3 days`; holiday_deposit 2026-09-16T21:40Z marian_prowse `2 hours`. Both runs then report `nothing further was scheduled at <that instant>`.
findings.why_it_matters: The reason string is false as a description of what happened -- something further was scheduled and code refused it -- and the refused item is exactly the evidence the runtime says licenses a NO. It is also unauditable: nothing in the artifacts a reviewer reads shows that an actor's next move was deleted, so a run in which everybody named a time past the deadline is indistinguishable from a run in which nobody had any plans at all.
findings.suggested_fix: Record every dropped wake and event as a trace entry written to code_overrides.jsonl, and let the earliest dropped instant feed the horizon test rather than being discarded.

findings.title: A YES taken at a budget or step truncation is reported as `resolved`
findings.evidence: trajectory.py:802-803 `elif answer["status"] == "YES": traj.status = "resolved"` ignores `truncated`, contradicting the same function's docstring at :770-773 (`Such a run is reported as incomplete and may still return YES on what it did commit`); run_simulation.py:105 then exits 0 for it. No run in final_v6 is affected -- all 8 YES verdicts were returned from the mid-loop check at :1005-1008 with reason empty.
findings.why_it_matters: A run that stopped because it ran out of steps or calls and then answered YES on what it had is indistinguishable, in the status field the summariser prints (evaluation/summarise_runs.py:42) and in the process exit code, from a run that finished cleanly. The YES itself is defensible; erasing the truncation is not.
findings.suggested_fix: Keep the `incomplete_*` status when the run was truncated and carry the YES in `answer`, so the status names how the run ended and the answer names what it found.

findings.title: No mechanical check on any terminal invariant, so a violated one would ship invisibly
findings.evidence: evaluation/verify_run.py:36-108 checks resolution leakage, unobserved items in views, time order, causes, duplicate descriptions, wake provenance and replay -- and nothing about the terminal. Nothing in it would flag a NO_AT_CUTOFF in a run whose ledger never reaches the cutoff, an `incomplete_*` status carrying a NO (reachable, see above), or a `supporting_event_ids` entry that is not a committed journal event of the trajectory. All 11 runs report `chk ok`.
findings.why_it_matters: The invariants are enforced inside the live process only. What a reviewer or a future maintainer actually reads is a frozen corpus, and PR #5's manufactured NOs were caught by humans reading traces rather than by any check. The one claim this branch exists to make is the one claim the shipped checks do not test.
findings.suggested_fix: Add to check(): NO_AT_CUTOFF implies the last ledger timestamp >= cutoff and status == "cutoff"; status.startswith("incomplete") implies answer != NO_AT_CUTOFF; and every supporting_event_id is a journal.event record of this trajectory_id.

findings.title: The test named for recording the horizon advance asserts nothing, and the safeguard it names is dead
findings.evidence: tests/test_semantic_runtime.py:1395-1431 asserts `len(advanced) <= 1` for `semantic.horizon_reached`, which zero satisfies, and its own docstring hedges that `there may be nothing to record`. There are 0 such records in all 11 runs of final_v6 and 0 in every configuration of my probe, including the ones that end `status=cutoff`, because `not truncated` already implies now >= cutoff -- so trajectory.py:785-793, and the comment at :787-790 explaining why the advance must be recorded, is unreachable code.
findings.why_it_matters: A reader takes the test name and the comment as evidence that the clock is never moved without a ledger record. Nothing moves the clock there, and if the reachability changed the test would not notice.
findings.suggested_fix: Either delete the advance and its record with the dead branch, or make the test assert exactly one horizon record in a case that genuinely needs the advance.
